questions.stem: What are the essential parts of an electromagnet?

options.text: a coil of wire carrying a current
options.explanation: Current through a coil is the core construction.

options.text: a permanent magnet glued to a wire
options.explanation: No permanent magnet is part of the construction.

options.text: a battery and a plastic rod
options.explanation: The plastic rod is non-magnetic and pointless as a core.

options.text: a single straight wire
options.explanation: A single wire's field is weak; coiling is the construction.

questions.stem: Why is the coil often wound on a soft iron core?

options.text: the core makes the electromagnet permanent
options.explanation: Soft iron is chosen because it is NOT permanent.

options.text: the core is induced by the coil's field and strengthens it
options.explanation: Induced magnetism in the core multiplies the field.

options.text: the core stores the electricity for later
options.explanation: Cores store no charge.

options.text: the core keeps the coil cool
options.explanation: Cooling is not the core's role.

questions.stem: The current through an electromagnet is reversed. What happens?

options.text: it becomes stronger
options.explanation: Reversal changes direction, not strength.

options.text: nothing observable changes
options.explanation: The pole swap is observable with a compass.

options.text: its poles swap ends
options.explanation: Reversed current reverses the field and the pole positions.

options.text: it switches off completely
options.explanation: A reversed current still runs — the magnet works with swapped poles.

questions.stem: Which change makes an electromagnet STRONGER?

options.text: removing the iron core
options.explanation: The core strengthens the field; removing it weakens the magnet.

options.text: reducing the current
options.explanation: A smaller current weakens the field.

options.text: unwinding the coil into a straight wire
options.explanation: Uncoiled wire gives a much weaker surrounding field.

options.text: adding more turns to the coil
options.explanation: More turns stack more field contributions.

questions.stem: A scrapyard electromagnet releases its load the moment the current stops. What property of the core makes this possible?

options.text: soft iron loses its induced magnetism as soon as the field goes
options.explanation: Soft-iron behaviour gives the on/off control.

options.text: the core is magnetically hard and holds its poles
options.explanation: A hard core would keep holding the load.

options.text: the core cools instantly
options.explanation: Release is magnetic, not thermal.

options.text: the coil unwinds slightly
options.explanation: The coil geometry is unchanged by switching off.

questions.stem: State what an electromagnet is made from.
questions.modelAnswer: A coil of wire, often wound around a soft iron core, carrying a current.

questions.stem: State when an electromagnet behaves as a magnet.
questions.modelAnswer: Only while a current flows through its coil.

questions.stem: Explain why reversing the current swaps the poles of an electromagnet.
questions.modelAnswer: Each turn of the coil produces a field whose direction is set by the current direction, and the turns stack into the end-to-end field of a bar-like magnet. Reversing the current reverses every turn's circulation, so the stacked field reverses along the axis — the end that was north becomes south and the poles swap.

questions.stem: A hospital needs a magnet that can hold a steel instrument during an operation and release it instantly on demand. Design the magnet and justify each choice.
questions.modelAnswer: Use an electromagnet: a many-turn coil on a soft iron core, supplied by a switchable current. The coil and core give a strong holding field while the current flows, and the soft core sheds its induced magnetism the instant the current is cut, releasing the instrument cleanly — a permanent magnet could do the holding but could never release on command.
